summary: Lawrence Jones introduces incident.io, an incident response management platform used by Netflix, Etsy, and Skyscanner, whose broader goal is to fully automate production investigations. These investigations run hundreds of telemetry queries across logs, metrics, traces, historical incident data, and code to produce root cause analyses. The complexity makes human debugging intractable: a single investigation may involve hundreds or thousands of prompts, and verifying correctness can take an hour of manual review. The talk assumes familiarity with core AI engineering constructs (prompts, evals, scorecards, traces, datasets, backtests) and presents three patterns for using AI to manage production AI system complexity. The first pattern treats evals as AI unit tests. Evals live in YAML files next to Go prompt definitions, specifying input data, the prompt, and grading criteria. Production evals can encompass an entire incident, making YAML files too large for coding agents to load into context. A small CLI tool lets agents query, edit, replace, and add eval cases without loading the full file, enabling a red-green runbook: write a failing eval, fix the prompt, verify no regressions, and consolidate. The second pattern addresses multi-prompt system hierarchies. The chatbot has 10+ agents and 50+ prompts/tools, and the investigation system is even more complex. Engineers struggle to identify which prompt caused a bad output. The solution: serialize every UI debugging view as a downloadable file system. Drop it into a Claude Code session, describe the bad behavior, and the agent traces through the prompt hierarchy to pinpoint exactly which prompt to change. Traces translate well to ASCII. The agent can then make the fix and verify it using the eval red-green cycle. The third pattern addresses fleet-scale analysis. The team runs thousands of investigations daily across hundreds of customer accounts via backtests, producing rolled-up accuracy numbers (e.g., 86% accurate RCA) that don't explain why performance changed. They built a repo called scrapbook with structured markdown playbooks. The pipeline launches 25 agents in parallel, each analyzing one investigation, then a second stage clusters results to surface systemic failure patterns and actionable recommendations. Analysis is stored in files for incremental resumability, and the pipeline combines analysis with the codebase so agents can identify both the problem and the fix. Jones emphasizes that file systems are exceptionally good agent context—better than MCP or human-use agents—because they allow bulk download and grep-based exploration.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and incident.io context
sections.summary: Lawrence Jones introduces himself as a founding engineer at incident.io, an incident response management platform. The company's goal extends beyond helping humans respond to incidents to fully automating production investigations, running hundreds of telemetry queries across logs, metrics, traces, historical data, and code. These systems are too complex for humans to debug unaided, and verifying a single investigation report can take an hour.

sections.title: Talk overview and assumptions
sections.summary: Jones references his prior LDX talk on becoming AI engineers and assumes familiarity with prompts, evals, scorecards, traces, datasets, and backtests. This talk covers three patterns: using AI to curate eval datasets, translating UI debugging views into downloadable file systems, and building repeatable AI agent analysis pipelines. He begins with evals.

sections.title: Evals as AI unit tests
sections.summary: Evals are defined as AI unit tests: each takes a prompt, input data, produces output, and applies grading criteria. At incident.io, evals live in YAML files next to Go prompt code. Jones demonstrates a contrived pirate-speak prompt with two grading criteria and three test cases, showing pass/fail results.

sections.title: Eval challenges and CLI tool solution
sections.summary: Evals are fiddly; production evals can include an entire incident, creating YAML files too large for coding agents to load into context. The team built a CLI tool ('eval tool') allowing agents to query, edit, replace, and add eval cases without loading the full file. This enables a red-green runbook: agent writes a failing eval, fixes the prompt, verifies all other evals still pass, and consolidates the prompt. Jones demonstrates this in Claude Code with a real log-query prompt.

sections.title: Multi-prompt system complexity
sections.summary: Jones pivots to the deeper problem: production AI systems are not single prompts but hierarchies of many agents, tools, and prompts. The incident.io chatbot has 10+ agents and 50+ prompts/tools. The investigation system is even more complex, with each trace step expanding into potentially hundreds of sub-steps. Even with the eval red-green cycle, engineers cannot easily identify which prompt in the hierarchy caused a bad output, motivating the patterns covered in the next section.

sections.title: File system serialization of UI debugging views
sections.summary: Jones describes the second pattern: serializing all UI debugging views as downloadable file systems. Inspired by Claude Code's effectiveness with file systems, the team made every AI interaction downloadable as a self-documenting file system that can be dropped into a Claude Code sandbox. The agent can see all prompt inputs, understand the system structure, and trace through the hierarchy to identify exactly which prompt to change. Traces translate well to ASCII. The workflow: download the bad interaction, ask Claude Code to diagnose, identify the fix, make the change in the codebase, and verify with the eval red-green cycle.

sections.title: Fleet-scale analysis pipeline
sections.summary: Jones addresses the fleet-scale problem: thousands of investigations run daily across hundreds of customer accounts. Backtests produce rolled-up accuracy numbers (e.g., 86% RCA accuracy) that don't explain why performance changed. The team built a repo called scrapbook with structured markdown playbooks. The pipeline launches 25 agents in parallel, each analyzing one investigation, then a second stage clusters results to surface systemic failure patterns and actionable recommendations. Key principles: leverage sub-agents for parallel per-entity analysis, store analysis in files for incremental resumability, and combine analysis with the codebase so agents can identify both the problem and the fix. The end result is a PR addressing the identified issues.

sections.title: Conclusion and key principles
sections.summary: Jones emphasizes that these patterns generalize to anyone building complex AI systems. Teams must use AI equally effectively in internal debugging tools as in their products. File systems are exceptionally good agent context—better than MCP or human-use agents—because they allow bulk download and grep-based exploration. Complex analysis should be captured as AI runbooks rather than performed ad hoc, saving days or weeks. He concludes with a hiring note for incident.io's London team.
